content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an editing tool for natural images, such as ImageNet, based on a diffusion model (DDPM). There are four types of editing, including backgrounds (controlling high-frequency pixels in the image) and information about objects such as sizes, positions, and directions. Specifically, background editing is based on DDPM where DDPM is guided by the amplitude of the high-frequency components of the given image. Object information editing first performs an in-painting method using the given mask (the reviewer presumes that masks are provided by the ImageNet-S dataset), while the masked object is resized/transposed/rotated by a linear transformation. Then the in-painted image and the transformed object are fed into DDPM. Based on this editing process, this paper proposes the ImageNet-E dataset: 47,872 images with 373 classes and five levels of complexity. Here, 373 classes are selected from "animal" classes, and 47,872 samples are selected from the ImageNet-S dataset (with mask annotations). The proposed dataset shows similar distribution to the original ImageNet dataset, while the other popular ImageNet robustness benchmarks show different distributions from the original ImageNet (Figure 5). Benchmark results show that in ImageNet-E, the existing methods perform worse than the standard accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength

- A new robustness benchmark with the in-distributed distribution. As shown in Table 5, the existing benchmarks often change the distribution significantly.
- A new robustness benchmark with a different point of view from the previous benchmarks (attribute editing)

## Weakness

### "Background editing" is not actually about the background

In the introduction, this paper provides an example of "background" as
> For example, it is interesting to explore whether a bird with a water background can be recognized correctly even if most birds appear with trees or grasses in the training data

However, the "background editing" in this paper is not actually about backgrounds with different contexts, but adding or removing high-frequency noise into the image using DDPM. In terms of the background context, I think this paper should compare the "Background challenge dataset" Xiao et al 2021 [R1]: this dataset mixes foregrounds and backgrounds of images to show that a model focuses on the foreground or the background (i.e., showing that there exists a spurious correlation between class and background). Although Xiao et al 2021 briefly mentioned in Section 5, I think this dataset should be discussed in detail (e.g., Figure 5).

[R1] Kai Xiao, Logan Engstrom, Andrew Ilyas, and Aleksander Madry. Noise or signal: The role of image backgrounds in object recognition. Proceedings of the International Conference on Learning Representations, 2021.

I think the "background editing" in this paper is more similar to the high-pass filter, low-pass filter, and XX-noises of the ImageNet-C dataset. This procedure controls high-frequency components of the image with a better and smarter manipulation technique.

### Mask annotations?

This paper needs mask annotations, but there is no detailed information on how the mask annotations are achievable.
> Since the number of masks provided in ImageNet-S in these classes is 4352, thus the number of images in each edited kind is 4352

I found this sentence in Appendix, and presume that ImageNet-S is the following paper (it is not cited in the paper)

[R2] Gao, Shang-Hua, et al. "Large-scale Unsupervised Semantic Segmentation." arXiv preprint arXiv:2106.03149 (2021).

Please check this and revise the paper accordingly.

Anyway, the proposed method needs a precise image mask. If we do not have a precise mask, then the proposed object information editing is not applicable. It limits the scale of the proposed benchmark dataset. It will be great to add a discussion on the relationship between the quality of the mask and the edited data (e.g., coarse masks or low-quality masks).

### Others

- The proposed method is highly dependent on the quality of DDPM. Although humans think DDPM results look very realistic, it does not guarantee that DDPM images are actually "in-distributed". For example, adversarial attacked images are imperceptible to humans, but it changes the network decision significantly. Hence, we may need more evidence that DDPM images are actually in-distributed, or at least, I recommend adding a discussion related to the DDPM image generation quality itself.
- The dataset only has 373 animal classes. If there exists a model that works specifically well in animal classes while performing worse in other classes, then measuring the model performance in this dataset could lead to a different result from measuring in the full classes.

## Questions

- In terms of OOD detection (Figure 5), I wonder how the following benchmark sets differ from the original dataset. Especially, if the "inpainted ImageNet-S" is detected as "in-distributed", then I think that the employed OOD detection metric is not suitable to be used as evidence of in-distributed / out-of-distributed distributions. Similarly, if mixed-rand is detected as in-distributed, then I think there should be more comparisons with Xiao et al. 2021 in this paper.
    - ImageNet-V2
    - Mixed-Rand of Xiao et al. 2021 (https://github.com/MadryLab/backgrounds_challenge)
    - Inpainted ImageNet-S (before applying DDPM) => object-removed in Figure 4
    - Adversarial attacked ImageNet (by strong adversaries such as AutoAttack or PGD)
- The ImageNet-E dataset only has 373 classes. How do the authors handle the case if a model predicts the given image out of 373 classes? Is it treated as just "wrong"? or is the softmax computed by only 373 classes?
- I wonder if it is possible to make ImageNet-E for the other 627 classes and whether the tendency will be consistent with the 373 classes ImageNet-E. If the quality of 627 classes is too bad, it would be great to add a discussion related to the quality of 627 classes (e.g., attaching failure cases of generated images)

## Other comments

- I don't think it is necessary, but it will be interesting to show more (publically available) models on the benchmark results. For example, different augmentation methods (Mixup, CutMix, ...), different architectures (e.g., from timm library), ...
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I think the quality of this paper has a large room for improvement. For example, in terms of English quality, this paper could be better: "synthesizing high quality persons" => "synthesizing a high-quality person image" (or high-quality "people" at least). Please polish the overall paper, focusing on grammar and fluency.

As a minor comment, I feel that figure, tables are too small. It is recommended to maintain the text size of the figures or tables as the same as the main text. Similarly, it seems that there are some `vspace` between paragraphs (e.g., before Section 5). I recommend avoiding using vspace.

I found that the reproducibility of this work is not very promising as is, but can be easily achievable. Two factors are required for reproducibility: the source code and masks are given. The source code is not included in the supplementary material (although README says there is a source code), but I don't think re-implementing the algorithm is difficult. There is no information on how we can get masks, but I presume it is provided by the ImageNet-S dataset (https://github.com/LUSSeg/ImageNet-S). I believe these can be easily fixed during the discussion period.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes a new robustness benchmark based on attribute editing. Although the new attribute editing is an interesting idea, I think the overall quality of the paper is marginally below the acceptance threshold. For example, "background editing" is not about backgrounds (while there already exists a work focusing on a spurious correlation by backgrounds -- Xiao et al 2021); the proposed method is heavily dependent on expensive mask annotations / the quality of DDPM. Please check "Weakness" for more details. I also think the quality of this paper can be improved. Overall, I think this paper is marginally below the acceptance threshold of the ICLR conference.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ACWD (1/3)
content.comment:
**Q1. The "background editing" and  Differences with "background challenge dataset".**

- Our "background editing" involves both editing the background's complexity and mix-rand backgrounds (Appendix, Section E). The background editing method differs from the high-pass filter or low-pass filter. In ImageNet-C, xx-noise can add some high-frequency components by adding noises to images. Therefore, images look noisier. In contrast, our method introduces a more informative background during the generation with DDPM, such as the messy branches in Figure1, row#3, column #3 in the background part. More examples can be found in Figure 9 (Compare images generated with $\lambda=-20$ and $\lambda=20$).
#
- We differ from ImageNet-9 in two aspects: 
    - Background editing method. In contrast to ImageNet-9 which conducts copy-paste to generate images, our method adopts the diffusion model to make the generated images more natural. As shown in  Figure 8, the images in ImageNet-9 contain some artifacts while ours look more natural. The results of mix-rand in terms of FID (34.99 vs. 15.57, ImageNet-9 vs. Ours) and OOD detection (overlaps: 0.6156 vs. 0.6709, ImageNet-9 vs. Ours) show that our generated images are more closed to the distribution of ImageNet. 

    - Dataset components. ImageNet-9 focuses on the background change while our ImageNet-E also contains other object attribute changes including object size, rotation, direction.

**Q2. Mask annotations.**

Thank you for your reminder. We have added the references in the revision. The proposed editing tool requires mask annotations as stated in our Limitation. We think combining some weakly supervised semantic segmentation methods may figure a way out to relieve this problem in future work.

**Q3. The DDPM image generation quality.**

Actually, the diffusion model DDPM is a parameterized Markov chain trained by variational reasoning to generate samples matching the distribution of the training dataset p(x) after a finite time. The image sampled by DDPM approximately falls into the ground-truth data distribution p(x). DDPM has achieved state-of-the-art image generation quality (Inception Score and Frechet Inception Distance). As for evaluating whether the generated images are in-distributed, we adopt some existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods including Energy (NeuraIPS2020) and GradNorm(NeuraIPS2021). These OOD detection methods aim to distinguish the OOD examples from the in-distribution examples. The experiment results demonstrate that images in ImageNet-E are actually close to/in the ImageNet distribution.

**Q4. If there exists a model that works specifically well in animal classes while performing worse in other classes, then measuring the model performance in this dataset could lead to a different result from measuring in the full classes.**

This is a good question. Though the performance tendency on the animal classes is in line with the tendency on the ImageNet validation set, one cannot ensure that there doesn't exist any model that works specifically well in animal classes while performing worse in other classes. And that's the reason why we choose the top-1 accuracy drop rate as the metric for evaluating the robustness based on the idea that attribute editing should induce little change to a robust model.

**Q5. How do the following benchmark sets differ from the original dataset? ImageNet-V2, Mixed-Rand, Inpainted ImageNet-S, Adversarial attacked ImageNet.**

We add these evaluations in the Appendix, Figure 15. With the OOD detection evaluation, it can be observed that the ImageNet-V2 is close to ImageNet while others not. The adversarial examples are generated with PGD under eps=16. The Energy (first row) method can distinguish it from ImageNet but GradNorm fails. However, In both metrics, our ImageNet-E shows the best proximity to the ImageNet. When compared to Mix-Rand in 'background challenge' dataset, our overlaps for random backgrounds under Energy and GradNorm metrics are 0.6709 and 0.9999 while they are 0.6156 and 0.8107.  This implies that our editing tool can give a controlled evaluation on object attribute changes.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ACWD (2/3)
content.comment:
**Q6. How do the authors handle the case if a model predicts the given image out of 373 classes? Is it treated as just "wrong"? or is the softmax computed by only 373 classes?**

We didn't add any post-process to the model output to simulate the real-world scenario, where the deployed model has no knowledge about how the input image is edited. Therefore, if a model predicts the given image out of 373 classes, it is treated as 'wrong'.

**Q7. If it is possible to make ImageNet-E for the other 627 classes and whether the tendency will be consistent with the 373 classes ImageNet-E.**

Thank you for your suggestion. This experiment can be found in our Appendix Section D.3. We extend the ImageNet-E to ImageNet-E-L, which contains 919 classes. The tendency is consistent with experiments on ImageNet-E, indicating that using our ImageNet-E can already reflect the model robustness against object attribute changes. We only keep the 373 classes due to the limitation induced by DDPM, which fails to generate high-quality person images. The failure cases of generated images are included in Figure 16 in the revision.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this work, the authors use diffusion models to “edit” examples of ImageNet in order to find vulnerabilities of vision models to changes in certain aspects of training data such as background, object size, and position. A collection of such examples is generated and named as the ImageNet-E dataset. Authors then show that vision models struggle to correctly predict labels on ImageNet-E and follow with strategies to mitigate this problem.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper lacks clarity of motivation (as pointed out in the previous section of the review), as well as clarity to state the purpose of each experiment. I also found it difficult to parse some results such as the plots in Figure 5 and the left-most plot in Figure 6.
- It seems to me that standard augmentations such as color jittering could be helpful to improve robustness against the perturbations found in ImageNet-E but I couldn’t find in the manuscript any information regarding the augmentations employed at training time in the experiments reported in Section 4.1.
- The metrics reported in Section 3.2 are key to support the main claim of the paper that ImageNet-E contains in-distribution perturbations with respect to ImageNet. However, it is not clear what exactly the reported metrics for out-of-distribution detection are accounting for (i.e. out-of-distribution in what sense?) and why the authors selected the two reported metrics. 
- The plots in Figure 5 do not have labels on the x-axis, which makes it hard to interpret them and judge the merits of the central claim of the paper. 
- I believe it is necessary to provide further experimental evidence to support the claim that ImageNet-E is “in-distribution” with respect to ImageNet. This can be done by, for example, including metrics that account for marginal shifts between ImageNet and ImageNet-E and baselines. For instance, the authors could consider the Frechet Inception Distance, Kernel Inception distance [1], and H-divergence [2] (i.e. train a binary classifier to distinguish between ImageNet and the compared datasets). 
- What is the goal of the experiment reported in Section 4.3? It is not clear to me why one would expect that l2 robustness could in any sense be helpful to improve robustness to the types of perturbations present in ImageNet-E. Also, could the results from this experiment be an artifact of a likely drop in clean accuracy when the perturbation budget increases? 
 
- Minor:
  - Section 4: Swin-Transformer(Swin) -> Swin-Transformer (Swin) 
  - Section 4.1: what exactly is a “normally” trained model?
  - Section 4.1: “for human beings, the change is imperceptible, as shown in Figure 1, row 3”, this does not seem to be the case, since it is possible to spot the differences between backgrounds by inspecting the figure.
 
[1] Bińkowski et al. "Demystifying MMD GANs.", 2018. \
[2] Ben-David et al. "A theory of learning from different domains.", 2010.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work introduced ImageNet-E, a synthetic dataset containing modified versions of ImageNet examples. Although I believe this line of work is very relevant for the machine learning community given that it can be used to diagnose failure modes of models, not only the proposed approach presents limitations (the types of perturbations are limited and object-of-interest masks must be available), but also the current version of the manuscript lacks in multiple aspects. More specifically, as pointed out in the previous Section of the review, the main motivation of the paper is not clear and it contains claims that were not properly supported by the presented evidence.

content.title: Response to Reviewer THGV (1/2)
content.comment:
**Q1. Why exactly is it important to debug the model with respect to in-distribution data?**

Please refer to the answer to generic comment #1.

**Q2. The claim of in-distribution data. Why do the authors select the two reported metrics? The x-axis in Figure 5. What about the Frechet Inception Distance?**
- One way for evaluating the similarity of two distributions can be KL divergence. However, the data distribution p(x) is hard to be measured.  As an alternative, we adopt some existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods including Energy (NeuraIPS2020) and GradNorm(NeuraIPS2021) following DRA (TIP 2022)[a]. These OOD detection methods aim to distinguish the OOD examples from the in-distribution examples. The results are shown in Fig.5, x-axis is the ID score and y-axis is the frequency of each ID score. A high ID score indicates the detection method takes the input sample as the in-distribution data (This description has been added in the revision). In Fig.5, higher overlap indicates greater proximity to ImageNet. Compared to other datasets, our ImageNet-E can get a higher overlap with ImageNet, indicating that our editing tool can ensure a better proximity to the original ImageNet.
#
- The Frechet Inception Distance for our ImageNet-E is 15.57 for random backgrounds, which is 34.99 for ImageNet-9 (background challenge), indicating that our ImageNet-E holds a better proximity than other background editing methods. This is consistent with the results evaluated with the OOD detection metric.

**Q3. Multiple runs.**

Thanks for the suggestion. We have conducted 5 runs of the algorithms with 5 seeds. All the results have been updated in the revision. Due to the space limits, we show the mean values in the main text.

**Q4. Standard augmentations that may be helpful to improve robustness against the perturbations found in ImageNet-E.**

Table 2 in the main text has provided a comparison in terms of different training strategies including Augmix and DeepAugment. In table 4 in the revision, we have also included an RN50 trained with lots of data augmentations from paper [e] (RN50-T). content.title: Response to Reviewer THGV (2/2)
content.comment:
**Q5. The adversarially trained models. Could the results from this experiment be an artifact of a likely drop in clean accuracy when the perturbation budget increases?**
- Section 4.3 is the "Bad case analysis". We think what you are confused about is the evaluation on "Adversarially trained models" in Section 4.1? Previous studies have found that adversarial training can improve the robustness not only on adversarial examples. For example, [b] found that "Although ALP was designed to increase robustness to small gradient perturbations, it markedly improves robustness to all sorts of noise, blur, weather, and digital IMAGENET-P perturbations—methods generalizing this well is a rarity. In point of fact, a publicly available Tiny ImageNet ResNet-50 model ﬁne-tuned with ALP has a 41% and 40% relative decrease in the mFP and mT5D on TINY IMAGENET-P,  respectively". The work in [c] also mentioned that "adversarial trained models can alleviate the texture bias and learn a more shape-biased representation" and this has been validated on ImageNet-R [d]. As one kind of adversarially trained models, we think it is necessary to evaluate the robustness of $L_2$ adversarially trained models on ImageNet-E. The evaluation of $L_\infty$ adversarially trained models has been added in the revision Figure 6.
#
- The results in Figure 6 show that adversarial training can hurt the model's robustness to attribute changes. To make comprehensive studies, we step further to evaluate the adversarially trained model's robustness under different perturbation budgets. We find that a small perturbation budgets (0.01) can help to improve the robustness to attribute changes slightly. In this paper, we aim to provide a model debugging method. We reveal that adversarially trained models may be more vulnerable than normal models in some scenarios and appeal to the community to reflect on current robustness practices in a more comprehensive way.
#
- It's true that adversarially trained models usually hold lower clean accuracy than normally(a.k.a standard) trained ones. Then the top-1 accuracy cannot reflect whether the model is robust to some extent. And that's the reason why we choose the top-1 accuracy drop rate instead of accuracy to relieve the influence of clean accuracy based on the idea that attribute editing should induce little change to a robust model. We have also provided the corresponding accuracies under different scenarios in Table 3,4,5,6, which show that the conclusion in terms of the absolute accuracy is consistent with that in terms of top-1 drop rate.

**Q6. "normally" trained models.**

The 'normally trained' is opposite to 'adversarial trained'. It indicates that the model is trained without the adversarial training strategy.

**Reference:**

Dear authors, thanks for your effort in the rebuttal and for addressing some of my comments.

The authors mentioned in the rebuttal that "The Frechet Inception Distance for our ImageNet-E is 15.57 for random backgrounds, which is 34.99 for ImageNet-9 (background challenge), indicating that our ImageNet-E holds a better proximity than other background editing methods." In addition to that, it is still unclear to me why the particular out-of-distribution detection methods employed in this work were selected and what type of distribution shifts they account for. 

As some of my comments were addressed, but critical concerns still remain, I decided to raise my score from 3 to 5.

content.title: Response to reviewer's response
content.comment:
Dear reviewer THGV:

    Thanks a lot for your time and response. While we are encouraged that some of your concerns have been addressed, we would like to make some further efforts to make our motivation and evaluation metric more comprehensive. 

    In this paper, based on the finding that higher accuracy on ImageNet usually leads to better robustness against different corruptions. We advocate that it is essential to promote the in-distribution performance on ImageNet in a bottom-up way, that is conducting model debugging with the in-distribution dataset to provide clues for model repairing and accuracy improvement. To achieve this goal, we generate the ImageNet-E.  

- OOD detection: In contrast to FID distance which indicates the divergence of two datasets, the OOD detection is used to indicate the extent of the deviance of a single input image from the in-distribution dataset. It has been adopted as the in-distribution measurement in many studies[a][b][c], including the ImageNet-A (Natural adversarial examples). In this paper, we aim to edit the object's attribute in the given image while maintaining it in the original distribution. Therefore, we think it is appropriate to choose the OOD detection as the evaluation method to find out whether the generated image is an in-distribution one.
#
- FID: Since our goal is to make the edited image in its original distribution instead of the whole dataset, the FID distance (15.57) can be greater than the distance (0.99) between the ImageNet test and validation set. For example, the FID between ImageNet and a dataset which consists of 100 copies of a randomly picked sample from ImageNet is 446.33. However, the extracted sample is an in-distribution one. Therefore, we think the FID may be inappropriate for evaluating whether the generated image is in-distribution or not. Still, the FID (15.57) of ImageNet is much smaller than that of ImageNet-A (50.25) and the background challenge (34.99). Moreover, paper [b] writes in its abstract that "This paper proposes the Chamfer OOD examples (CODEs), whose distribution is close to that of in-distribution samples". While it also claims that the distribution of their generated data is close to that of in-distribution samples, its FID is 36.53, much greater than 15.57. Therefore, we think it is ok to say make this statement that "ImageNet-E holds a better proximity than other background editing methods". 
#
- Overall, the concept of 'in distribution" in our paper is for samples (single image in imagenet-e), not datasets (imagenet-e). We have added the above explanation and revised our paper to make the description more rigorous.

Please let us know whether we have addressed your concerns.

[a] Hendrycks et al., "Natural Adversarial Examples", CVPR 2021.

[b] Tang, Keke, et al. "CODEs: Chamfer Out-of-Distribution Examples against Overconfidence Issue." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2021.

[c] Y. Zhu et al., "Toward Understanding and Boosting Adversarial Transferability From a Distribution Perspective," in IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, vol. 31, pp. 6487-6501, 2022, doi: 10.1109/TIP.2022.3211736.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a dataset for robustness evaluation and analysis of trained computer vision models. The ImageNet validation set was modified to edit the background, sizes and position/direction of objects using a process involving object bounding boxes, and image inpainting based on diffusion models. The resulting dataset is supposingly iid (as image statistics match the one of the original ImageNet validation set) in contrast to other robustness benchmarks such as ImageNet-A, C, etc.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

- The dataset and generation scheme are interesting, and a dataset like ImageNet-E is needed in the robustness community.

## Major Weaknesses

- The baseline experiments are insufficient, and there is a number of recent computer vision models missing in the evaluation. Given the size of the dataset, it would be easy to add additional baselines and reference results to the paper.
- The proposed metric (which is a relative improvement) might be insufficient/unclear. I am happy to discuss this point further, but what is the motivation for not also showing the absolute accuracies?
- There are insufficient controls for the "iid" claim the authors make. I have two actionable suggestions:
    - Batch norm adaptation: This check is very simple to compute. E.g. for the models in Table 2, compute the full adaptation results using batch norm adaptation (see Schneider et al., NeurIPS 2020). If the dataset is truly iid, the adaptation results should not be signficantly better than the ground truth (except potentially for the background changes, but see my comment below). Seeing a proof-of-concept result for the ResNet50 model here would already be interesting.
    - Cycle consistency: For the transformations, a better control is needed. I propose to apply the "inverse transformation" to each image in the dataset (e.g., shift the object back into their original positions) and compute the resulting accuracy. If no significant degradation was induced by the diffusion model, the resulting score should also be insiginficantly different from the clean dataset. I could imagine that this will actually not be the case, and the diffusion model degrades the images (similar to a corruption). If that is the case, I think that this is fine and expected, but then the achievable baseline accuracy is *not* the "clean" ImageNet accuracy, but the "cycle-consistency" accuracy of generating the original clean image using the diffusion model. Also, the authors would need to tune down the iid claim they make prominently at multiple locations in the paper. I am happy to debate this point/control experiment.
- When editing the background, it is not clear to me how the data can be considered "iid". The background have no clear relationships toward the original ImageNet backgrounds. Could you explain the reasoning here?
- Correctness: "Adversarial training is the state-of-the-art method for improving the adversarial robustness of deep neural networks"
    - This needs a citation that is more up to date.
    - I think it is logically wrong/not obvious to conclude that adversarial robustness = perturbation robustness. If the authors work with this hypothesis, they should cite a reference.
    - Given the prev point, it is not "surprising" that adversarially trained models are not very effective against ImageNet-E. Could the authors clarify why they expected this to be the case?
- "Extensive evaluations conducted on different state-of-the-art models show that most models are vulnerable to attribute changes, especially the adversarially trained ones"
    - Two important state of the art models on robustness benchmarks are missing, namely CLIP and the Noisy Student EfficientNet L2. CLIP claimed SOTA robustness results on most robustness benchmarks except ImageNet-C, while the Noisy Student model is (to the best of my knowledge) still the SOTA model on ImageNet-C and ImageNet-A. The authors should either **really** evaluate the SOTA models, or drop this claim/clarify from the text.
- All results should include mean and standard deviations over multiple runs of the algorithm. To have solid reference results I would propose 5 seeds, but 3 seeds would be fine as well.

Here is a list of computer vision models worth evaluating:
    - The entire `torchvision` library, which contains a lot of common models that might be useful when others use the benchmark.
    - A subset of relevant state-of-the art models; a suggestion could be to use models from the [timm](https://github.com/rwightman/pytorch-image-models) library.

Questions:
- Why is the dataset considered "iid"? How do the authors justify their notion of iid? One answer per transformation type (background, size, position/direction) would be great.
- "We further discover ways for robustness enhancement from both pre-processing, network designing and training strategies": Which specific ways did you discover?

## Minor Weaknesses

- There are multiple plots in the paper using the Jet colormap which is well-known to misrepresent the data. A colormap like viridis would be the better choice (but any perceptually uniform map would be fine). Could you adapt the plots accordingly?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity: 
    - paper is well written
    - the presentation of the key results is poor. From only looking at the tables, it is hard to infer the key results because there are a lot of numbers. A few well-made summary plots could help (on top of the tables, which are great as reference results for follow up work).

- Quality:
    - lacks rigorous evaluations that I would expect of a purely empirical ICLR paper. In particular, the paper lacks a larger scale analysis of more recent computer vision models.

- Novelty:
    - The approach for generating the benchmark is overall novel. However, the authors fail to prominently cite the [backgrounds challenge](https://github.com/MadryLab/backgrounds_challenge) which is the oldest paper I know that evaluates robustness to background changes.

- Reproducibility:
    - The paper is lacking references to code and model weights that were used for evaluation. These are crucial to include in the paper to facilitate reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The need for a dataset like ImageNet-E is clear, and I like the outlined approach for creating it. Because we are discussing a dataset paper, what is lacking most is experimental insight, and a thorough analysis of a range of state of the art and reference computer vision models. It would be good if the authors considered a wider range of models in their evaluation.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

**Q1. SoTA models such as CLIP and Noisy Student EfficientNet L2.**

We choose SoTA models in terms of validation accuracy on ImageNet validation set while taking training data and the model size into consideration as we have found that larger networks can help to improve the attribute robustness in Section 4.1. While CLIP and Noisy student models are trained with extra data which may make the evaluation unfair, we think it is still interesting to explore these SoTA models. Therefore, we also included evaluations and analysis of other SoTA models such as CLIP and Noisy Student EfficientNet L2 (EF-L2-NT) in the revision in Appendix, Section G. The results below indicate that ViT-B based CLIP is not as robust as the supervised trained ViT-B. We think that CLIP has spared some capacity for out-of-distribution robustness. While the previous study[a] has shown that zero-shot model of CLIP shows better out-of-distribution robustness than its finetuned one, it is not the case on ImageNet-E just like cases on ImageNet and ImageNet-V2. content.title: Response to Reviewer mvB1 (2/3)
content.comment:
**Q3. How do the authors justify their notion of in-distribution? Test batch norm adaptation and cycle consistency. When the background changes, how the data can be considered as 'iid'.**

- Evaluation with OOD and Frechet Inception Distance: One way for evaluating the similarity of two distributions can be KL divergence. However, the data distribution p(x) is hard to be measured.  As an alternative, we adopt some existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods including Energy (NeuraIPS2020) and GradNorm(NeuraIPS2021) following DRA (TIP 2022)[b]. These OOD detection methods aim to distinguish the OOD examples from the in-distribution examples.  The results are shown in Fig.5, x-axis is the ID score and y-axis is the frequency of each ID score. A high ID score indicates the detection method takes the input sample as the in-distribution data, therefore, the ImageNet data are on the right side (This description has been added in the revision). In Fig.5, higher overlap indicates greater proximity to ImageNet. Compared to other datasets, our ImageNet-E can get a higher overlap with ImageNet, indicating that our editing tool can ensure the proximity to the original ImageNet. Besides, the Frechet Inception Distance for our ImageNet-E is 15.57 for random backgrounds, which is 34.99 for ImageNet-9 (background challenge), indicating that our ImageNet-E holds better proximity than other background editing methods. This is consistent with the results evaluated with the OOD detection metric.
#
- BatchNorm adaptation(BNA). We have tested the full adaptation results using BNA on ResNet50. In contrast to the promotion on other out-of-distribution datasets, we find that this operation induces little changes to top-1 accuracy on both the ImageNet validation set (0.7615->0.7613) and our ImageNet-E (0.7935->0.7933 under $\lambda=20$ scenario, 0.6521->0.6514 under random position scenario, mean accuracy of 5 runs).  This similar tendency implies that our ImageNet-E shares a similar property with ImageNet.
#
- Cycle consistency. This is an interesting question. In fact, we have conducted the inverse transformation with $\lambda=0$ (we have renamed it as 'Inver' in the revision) in Table 1 and 2 to find out whether the diffusion model can induce some degradation. This operation will add some noises to the input image and then denoise it. It can be observed in both tables that degradation is negligible compared to degradation induced by attribute changes.


**Q4. When the background changes, how the data can be considered as 'iid'.**

In this paper, our effort aims to give an editable image tool that can conduct model debugging with in-distribution data. The overlaps in ID evaluation on images whose object's backgrounds are randomly shuffled are 0.6709/0.9999 for Energy/GradNorm. Compared to other benchmarks including ImageNet-C(0.4414/0.6378) and ImageNet-9(mix-rand backgrounds)(0.6156/0.8107), our generated data shows the best proximity (high overlaps) to the original ImageNet. We updated the statement carefully to make our paper more rigorous.

content.title: Response to Reviewer mvB1 (3/3)
content.comment:
**Q5. The reason for evaluating adversarially training models.**

- "Adversarial training is one of the most effective approaches for deep learning models to defend against adversarial examples." as summarized in [c]. Thus, we think it is reasonable to give the description in our paper that "Adversarial training is the state-of-the-art method for improving the adversarial robustness of deep neural networks". Note that what we mentioned is "adversarial robustness" not "perturbation robustness". 
#
- Previous studies have found that adversarial training can improve the robustness not only on adversarial examples. For example, [d] found that "Although ALP was designed to increase robustness to small gradient perturbations, it markedly improves robustness to all sorts of noise, blur, weather, and digital IMAGENET-P perturbations—methods generalizing this well is a rarity. In point of fact, a publicly available Tiny ImageNet ResNet-50 model ﬁne-tuned with ALP has a 41% and 40% relative decrease in the mFP and mT5D on TINY IMAGENET-P,  respectively". The work in [e] also mentioned that "adversarial trained models can alleviate the texture bias and learn a more shape-biased representation" and this has been validated on ImageNet-R [f].
#
- Taking the above findings into consideration, we think it is necessary to evaluate the robustness of adversarially trained models on our ImageNet-E for a comprehensive study. In this paper, we aim to provide a model debugging method. We reveal that adversarially trained models may be more vulnerable than normal models in some scenarios and appeal to the community to reflect on current robustness practices in a more comprehensive way. We have added the above analysis and references in the revision.


**Q6. Robustness enhancement.**

As detailed in Section 4.2, based on the evaluation results, we step further to discover ways to enhance the attribute robustness in terms of preprocessing (Ten-Crop), network design (attention module ) and training strategies (masked image modeling). More details can be found in Appendix D.5. 

**Q7. Multiple runs.**

Thanks for the suggestion. We have conducted 5 runs of the algorithms with 5 seeds. All the results have been updated in the revision. Due to the space limits, we show the mean value in the main text. 

**Q8. Citation of the background challenge.**

The dataset in background challenge is also known as ImageNet-9, which has been cited and discussed in our related work.

**Reference:**

[a] Kumar A, Raghunathan A, Jones R, et al. Fine-tuning can distort pretrained features and underperform out-of-distribution[J]. ICLR, 2022.

[b] Y. Zhu et al., "Toward Understanding and Boosting Adversarial Transferability From a Distribution Perspective," in IEEE Transactions on Image Processing, vol. 31, pp. 6487-6501, 2022, doi: 10.1109/TIP.2022.3211736.

[c] Bai, Tao, et al. "Recent advances in adversarial training for adversarial robustness." IJCAI (2021).

[d] Hendrycks, Dan, and Thomas Dietterich. "Benchmarking neural network robustness to common corruptions and perturbations." ICLR (2019).

[e] Zhang, Tianyuan, and Zhanxing Zhu. "Interpreting adversarially trained convolutional neural networks." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2019.

[f] Hendrycks, Dan, et al. "The many faces of robustness: A critical analysis of out-of-distribution generalization." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2021.

The whole attribute editing pipeline contains three steps: object-removal for pure backgrounds ($\mathbf{x}^b$)  with inpainting strategy, editing the foreground object to the desired attribute ($\mathbf{x}^o$) , fusing ($\mathbf{x}^b$) and ($\mathbf{x}^o$)

The cycle-consistency~(first inpaint for pure backgrounds then fusing with DDPM, finally treat the resulted image as the initial image and repeat the above procedure to put the objects back to its original position) can be viewed as a procedure that edits the image twice with the whole pipeline. The degradation is enlarged as expected since the result in 'Inver' column has shown that a single run of the whole procedure will introduce some degradation. content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper introduces a new benchmark ImageNet-E to measure robustness to changes in object attributes. The authors first introduce an object editing tool to generate images with changed attributes without changing the image’s semantic meaning.  A diffusion model is used to generate images with background, size, direction and position changes.

Unlike ImageNet-C, this is meant to focus on in-distribution debugging and, therefore, improve clean accuracy. The authors go on to show how the distribution of ImageNet-E overlaps significantly with the original ImageNet data unlike other benchmarks (ImageNet-C etc) using out of distribution detection methods.

Evaluation is done on CNN and transformer-based models. The authors find that all models experience large drops in performance when tested against attribute perturbations although larger models seem to do better. Adversarially trained models seem to do even worse than vanilla models when changing attributes such as background and size.

Finally, the authors show that some models (like SIN) perform well on benchmarks such as ImageNet-C but do poorly on ImageNet-E thus demonstrating the need for a new benchmark on attribute robustness.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper is well written and all concepts are explained well and sequenced in a logical manner.
2. This is significant problem to the community. I would like to thank the authors on making a solid first step in standardizing robustness evaluation on ImageNet for object attributes and promising to release the object editor publicly.
3. The experiments in the paper are thorough and support the conclusions the authors are trying to make.

Weaknesses:
1. I feel like the paper lacks analysis of where such a benchmark is useful. The authors briefly mention SIN as one model where existing benchmarks fail and ImageNet-E does well. However, I would have liked to see more such examples in addition to where and how these failure modes happen. 
2. Additionally, I felt that a lot of the analysis was focussed on examples related to changing backgrounds (including SIN) but we already have existing literature talking about this (Geirhos et al., which the authors do cite to be fair). In Section 4.2, examples of troubleshooting problems in a model are given but they are mostly focussed on background. Analysis on more complex transformations which are harder to study without access to an object editor such as pose etc would have enhanced the paper further. As it stands, the paper makes some interesting observations but none of them are “surprising”. (I fully admit that this is subjective)
3. Since the benchmark itself relies on another DL model (diffusion), I would have liked to see some discussion on the limitations of the benchmark itself. For example, do blindspots in the generator overestimate robustness in certain classes/attributes?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
To my knowledge, there is currently no benchmark to measure robustness on ImageNet with respect to object attributes. Being able to benchmark robustness and compare and contrast across models on standard datasets like ImageNet is a very important problem and I commend the authors on tackling it. 

The writing is good overall except where a few things are not defined before use. 

For example, the mask M in Algorithm 1 is left unexplained. It is only in the conclusion that we are told that the paper assumes object masks to be available. I think the authors should make this assumption clearer at the start.

The term “drop rate” is used without definition (or even a reference to the definition in Appendix D). Again, the meaning becomes clear from the context later but it is still a little jarring.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, I think the authors have identified an important problem and this is good first step at trying to get a handle on evaluating robustness on object attributes. However, I think the paper lacks more analysis about where such a benchmark is useful beyond a few well studied cases so I cannot recommend publication at this time.

content.title: Response to Reviewer g57E
content.comment:
**Q1. The usage of the benchmark.**

Please refer to the answer to generic comment #1 for the usage of the benchmark.

**Q2. More failure examples and where and how these failure modes happen. Analysis on more complex transformations.**

- In this paper, with comprehensive evaluations and analysis, we find that vision models can be vulnerable to object attribute changes. And more experimental results show that: 
    - Larger network can help to improve robustness (Section 4.1). 
    - Models that show good robustness on out-of-distribution datasets may show worse attribute robustness than vanilla models (Section 4.2).
    - Objects with tentacles are more easily to be attacked with complex backgrounds (Appendix, Section D.2). 
    - Attention Module and masked image modelling can help to improve the model's attribute robustness. (Section 4.3 and D.5)
    - The texture information is essential for tiny object classification, which is witnessed with the failure case analysis on more complex transformations where size editing,direction editing are all considered (Appendix D.4).
    - Model repairing based on the insights provided with evaluations on ImageNet-E can help to improve the out-of-distribution robustness as stated in the answer to generic comment #1 (Appendix, Section H).


**Q3. Limitations induced by the adopted diffusion models.**

Please refer to the answer to generic comment #2.

**Q4. Mask M and the term drop rate.**

Thank you for your reminder. We have updated the illustration of M in Section 3.2 and drop rate of top-1 accuracy in Section 4.1 in the main text to improve its readability.

content.title: Revision and generic comments
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their constructive comments and insightful suggestions. We carefully revised the manuscript according to the comments of all the reviewers. For convenience, we highlighted the revised text in blue color except for the revision of grammars. Here we briefly summarize the updates we have made to the revision:

- check and revise the grammatical and semantic errors of the entire paper carefully in the revision to improve its readability.
- cite and discuss the papers the reviewers provided.
- re-describe Figure 5 to make it more understandable.
- update all the results with the mean value of five runs.
- add a detailed discussion on the distribution in the Appendix, Section F.
- add further evaluation results on more state-of-the-art models in Appendix, Section G.
- add an example for model repairing based on the insights provided by evaluations on ImageNet-E in Appendix, Section H.

We have concluded all the comments from all the reviewers and responded to the generic comments as follows:
 
_**#1 Motivation and the dataset values.**_

**Response**: 
- **Motivation**. Most of the existing work builds datasets for evaluating the model robustness and generalization ability on out-of-distribution data. They have shown that higher accuracy on ImageNet usually leads to better robustness against different corruptions. Therefore, it is of great importance to promote the in-distribution performance on ImageNet, besides exploring a new domain that models may confront. However, most previous studies try to achieve this in a top-down way, such as architecture designing, exploring a better training strategy, etc. We advocate that it is also essential to manage it in a bottom-up way, that is conducting model debugging with the in-distribution dataset to provide clues for model repairing and accuracy improvement. Therefore, we create a toolkit for object editing with controls of backgrounds, sizes, positions, and directions, and create a rigorous benchmark named ImageNet-E(diting) for evaluating the image classifier robustness in terms of object attributes.
#
- **Example**. To validate that the evaluation on ImageNet-E can help to provide some insights for the model's applicability and enhancement, we conduct a toy example for model repairing. Our evaluation shows that the ResNet50 is vulnerable to background changes. Based on this observation, we randomly replace the backgrounds of objects during training and get a validation accuracy boost from 77.48% to 79.00%. It also improves the attribute robustness. For example, the top-1 accuracy and the accuracy drop rate are 0.8701 and 7.70% while they are 0.8549 and 8.83% for the vanilla model. Note that the promotion is not small as we only conduct this operation on 8781 training images (that's all the images with available mask annotations from ImageNet-S). We also step further to find out if the improved model can get a boost on other robustness benchmarks, as shown in the Table below. All results are top-1 accuracies(%) on corresponding datasets except for ImageNet-C(IN-C), which is mCE (mean corruption error). Higher top-1 accuracy and lower mCE indicate better performance. It can be observed that with the insights provided by the evaluation on ImageNet-E, one can explore the model's attribute vulnerabilities and struggle to repair the model and get a performance boost accordingly in both validation accuracy and out-of-distribution robustness.

    Table a.  Model repair results. All results are top-1 accuracies(%) on corresponding datasets except for ImageNet-C, which is evaluated by mCE.
    | Model| IN-val| IN-V2| IN-A| IN-C(mCE$\downarrow$)| IN-R| IN-Sketch | IN-E-bg-random | IN-E-size-0.05
    | ---| ---| ---| ---| ---| ---| ---| ---| ---|
    | ResNet50 | 77.5 | 65.7 | 6.5| 68.6| 39.6| 27.5| 85.5 | 76.8 |
    | ResNet50(**repaired**) | **79.0** | **67.2** | **9.4**| **65.8**| **40.7**| **29.4**| **87.0**| **79.1**|


_**#2 The limitation induced by the diffusion model.**_

- **The limitation induced by DDPM**. We find that synthesizing high-quality person images is difficult for DDPMs. In considering both the annotated mask and data quality, our ImageNet-E is a compact test set, as described in our Limitation.
#
- **Is there any bias or degradation induced by DDPM?** To find out whether the DDPM will induce some degradation to our evaluation, we have conducted experiments in both Table 1 and 2 with $\lambda=0$ (We have renamed it as 'Inver' in the revision). That is, adding noises to the original for $t_0$ steps and denoising it in the reverse diffusion process. It can be observed in both tables that degradation is negligible compared to the degradation induced by attribute changes.
